o: We concatenate some of our x copies of "AA", y copies of "BB", z copies of "AB", avoiding "AAA"/"BBB" substrings, maximizing total length (each piece has length 2). Example 1 (x=2,y=5,z=1) reaches 12; Example 2 (x=3,y=2,z=2) reaches 14. Key structural fact: "AB" can be inserted anywhere (its boundary A|B never creates a forbidden triple), while "AA" and "BB" pieces must alternate to avoid triples. So we can alternate min(x,y) pairs of AA/BB, and if x≠y one extra piece of the majority kind can terminate the sequence.
k: "AB" pieces are universally insertable — they never create AAA or BBB at any seam.
AA and BB pieces must strictly alternate, so together they contribute 2·min(x,y) pairs, plus one extra majority piece if x≠y.

a.i: Alternate AA/BB 2·min(x,y) times; if one of x,y is larger, append one extra piece of the abundant kind at the outer end (e.g., ...AABBAA ends with A, so an extra AA fits). Sprinkle all z "AB" pieces anywhere. Hence the closed-form answer.

a.n: Approach 2: Memoized DP over (counts, last char)
a.i: State f(a,b,c,last) = max pieces appendable given remaining counts and the last character placed. "AA" is forbidden iff last=='A', "BB" iff last=='B', "AB" is always legal (it ends in B, and A-after-A only forms "AA", never "AAA"). Only the last character matters, so the state space is tiny (≤ 51³·3).
s: Try placing AA (if last≠'A'), BB (if last≠'B'), AB (always).
a.t: O(x·y·z) ≤ 125000 states — each expands to 3 transitions.

w: In an interview, derive the formula with the exchange/insertion argument, then optionally validate with the DP. Pitfall: thinking "AB" can't follow an 'A' — it can, since "AAB" has no triple. The DP also generalizes to arbitrary piece sets, which is a natural follow-up.
